summary: This is Emil Kowalski's design-engineering agent skill: a compact rulebook for UI polish, animation decisions and component details. It gives a four-step framework for any animation (should it animate, why, which easing, how fast) with a frequency table, an easing decision tree, three custom cubic-bezier curves and a duration table capped at 300ms for UI. It adds concrete component rules (press scale 0.97, never scale(0), origin-aware popovers, instant subsequent tooltips), spring, gesture and performance rules, reduced-motion and touch-hover handling, the principles behind Sonner, stagger and debugging practice, and a review checklist. For a design system these become motion tokens, component behaviour defaults and a locked review checklist.
key_ideas: Taste is trained by studying and reverse engineering great interfaces.
Invisible details compound; people love interfaces without knowing why.
Decide whether to animate by how often people see the element; frequent or keyboard actions get no animation.
Every animation needs a purpose: spatial consistency, state, explanation, feedback or avoiding jarring change.
Easing follows the job: ease-out to enter or exit, ease-in-out to move, ease for hover, linear for constant motion, never ease-in.
Built-in CSS easings are too weak; use strong custom curves.
UI animation stays under 300ms, and speed shapes perceived performance.
Springs suit gestures and interruptible motion because they keep velocity; keep bounce subtle.
Pressable things scale to about 0.97; nothing enters from scale(0); popovers grow from their trigger, modals from center.
Transitions beat keyframes for rapidly triggered UI because they retarget instead of restarting.
Animate only transform and opacity; prefer CSS or WAAPI when the main thread is busy.
Reduced motion means fewer and gentler animations, not zero.
Loved components come from low-friction setup, excellent defaults, invisible edge-case handling and cohesive motion.
Be slow where the user decides and fast where the system responds.
Debug motion in slow motion, frame by frame, on real devices and the next day.

topics.name: Motion principles
topics.summary: A four-step decision framework (should it animate, purpose, easing, speed), frequency-based rules, valid purposes, no scale(0), cohesion with component personality, and asymmetric timing.

topics.name: Easing and timing
topics.summary: Easing decision tree by job, three custom cubic-bezier tokens, never ease-in, a duration table per element type, a 300ms cap for UI, exits faster than entrances, and 30-80ms stagger.

topics.name: Spring animation
topics.summary: When to use springs, useSpring for decorative mouse tracking, Apple duration+bounce config recommended over mass/stiffness/damping, subtle bounce 0.1-0.3, and velocity-preserving interruption.

topics.name: Animation performance
topics.summary: Animate only transform and opacity, avoid inherited CSS variable updates during drag, Framer Motion shorthands are main-thread, CSS animations beat JS under load, and WAAPI for programmatic control; blur under 20px.

topics.name: Gestures and drag
topics.summary: Velocity-based dismissal above ~0.11, damping and friction at boundaries, pointer capture, multi-touch protection, and testing gestures on real devices.

topics.name: Micro-interactions
topics.summary: Press scale 0.97 on :active, blur to mask crossfades, hold-to-delete with clip-path, clipped tab color transitions and comparison sliders.

topics.name: Reduced motion
topics.summary: Reduced motion means fewer and gentler animations, keeping opacity and color while removing movement; useReducedMotion in React.

topics.name: Accessibility
topics.summary: Motion sickness risk and reduced motion, plus gating hover animations behind (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine) for touch devices.

topics.name: Toasts and notifications
topics.summary: Toasts enter and exit from the same direction, use transitions rather than keyframes, pause timers when the tab is hidden, fill stack gaps to keep hover, and Sonner's slower ease-based motion.

topics.name: Drawers and sheets
topics.summary: iOS-like drawer curve, translateY(100%) hiding, 200-500ms duration, damping and friction when dragging past the top, and avoiding inherited CSS variables during swipe.

topics.name: Modals and popovers
topics.summary: Popovers and tooltips scale from their trigger via var(--transform-origin); modals stay centered; tooltip delay then instant subsequent tooltips.

topics.name: Buttons and actions
topics.summary: Buttons scale to 0.97 on press with a 160ms ease-out transform, and hold-to-delete uses a slow press and snappy release.

topics.name: Feedback, empty and loading states
topics.summary: Faster-spinning spinners make loading feel faster; transitions prevent jarring appear/disappear changes.

topics.name: Design taste and judgement
topics.summary: Taste is trained, unseen details compound, and beauty is leverage in software.

topics.name: Design process
topics.summary: Answer the framework before coding, review the next day, slow motion and frame-by-frame inspection, real-device testing, and Before/After/Why review tables.

topics.name: UI libraries
topics.summary: Sonner principles for building loved components: minimal setup, great defaults over options, memorable naming, invisible edge cases, transitions for dynamic UI, and interactive docs.

topics.name: Design systems and tokens
topics.summary: Named easing tokens (--ease-out, --ease-in-out, --ease-drawer) and per-element duration ranges suitable as motion tokens.

topics.name: Web implementation (CSS and React)
topics.summary: @starting-style with a data-mounted fallback, percentage translates, 3D transforms, clip-path inset techniques, WAAPI, useInView and IntersectionObserver.

claims.claim: In a world where everyone's software is good enough, taste is the differentiator.
claims.evidence: You are a design engineer with the craft sensibility.

claims.claim: Good taste is a trained instinct, not personal preference or something innate.
People select tools based on the overall experience, not just functionality.
Animation on actions repeated hundreds of times a day makes them feel slow, delayed and disconnected.
Built-in CSS easings are too weak to make animations feel intentional.
A dropdown with ease-in at 300ms feels slower than one with ease-out at 300ms, because ease-in delays the initial movement.
claims.evidence: Never use ease-in for UI animations.

claims.claim: A faster-spinning spinner makes loading feel faster even when load time is identical.
ease-out at 200ms feels faster than ease-in at 200ms because the user sees immediate movement.
Springs feel more natural than duration-based animations because they simulate real physics and have no fixed duration.
Springs maintain velocity when interrupted, while CSS animations and keyframes restart from zero.
The default transform-origin: center is wrong for almost every popover.
CSS transitions can be interrupted and retargeted mid-animation; keyframes restart from zero.
claims.evidence: Use CSS transitions over keyframes for interruptible UI

claims.claim: Blur during a crossfade blends old and new states so the eye perceives one smooth transformation instead of two objects swapping.
Heavy blur is expensive, especially in Safari.
@starting-style replaces the React pattern of setting mounted: true in useEffect after the first render.
Percentage values in translate() are relative to the element's own size.
scale() scales an element's children too, unlike width/height, so text and icons scale with a pressed button.
Clipping a duplicated, active-styled tab list creates a color transition that timing individual color transitions can never achieve.
A clip-path comparison slider needs no extra DOM elements and is fully hardware-accelerated.
Without multi-touch protection, switching fingers mid-drag makes the element jump to the new position.
Transform and opacity skip layout and paint and run on the GPU; animating padding, margin, height or width triggers all three rendering steps.
Changing a CSS variable on a parent recalculates styles for all its children.
Framer Motion's x, y and scale shorthands are not hardware-accelerated; they use requestAnimationFrame on the main thread.
At Vercel, a dashboard tab animation using Shared Layout Animations dropped frames during page loads, and switching to CSS animations fixed it.
CSS animations run off the main thread and stay smooth when the browser is busy loading a page.
claims.evidence: CSS animations beat JS under load

claims.claim: The Web Animations API is hardware-accelerated, interruptible and needs no library.
claims.evidence: Use WAAPI for programmatic CSS animations

claims.claim: Animations can cause motion sickness.
Touch devices trigger hover on tap, causing false positives.
Most users never customize a component's defaults.
claims.evidence: Good defaults matter more than options.

claims.claim: Sonner's animation is slightly slower than typical UI animation and uses ease rather than ease-out to feel more elegant.
There is no formula for combining opacity and height animations on list items; it takes trial and error.
Imperfections missed during development are noticed when reviewing the next day.
claims.evidence: Review your work the next day

quotes: Reduced motion means fewer and gentler animations, not zero.
Good defaults matter more than options.

rules.rule: Study why the best interfaces feel the way they do: reverse engineer their animations and inspect their interactions instead of stopping once the UI works.
rules.why: Taste is a trained instinct, built by surrounding yourself with great work, thinking about why it feels good and practising.

rules.rule: Make every feature behave exactly as people assume it will, so they carry on without giving it a second thought.
rules.why: Most details are never consciously noticed; the aggregate of invisible correctness is what makes people love an interface.

rules.rule: Treat good defaults and good animations as a product differentiator, not an afterthought.
rules.why: People choose tools on the overall experience, and beauty is underused in software, so it is leverage to stand out.

rules.rule: When reviewing UI code, report findings as one markdown table with Before | After | Why columns, one row per issue; never as separate 'Before:' and 'After:' lines.
rules.why: The skill marks this format as required and shows the line-by-line format as wrong.

rules.rule: Before writing any animation code, answer in order: should it animate at all, what is its purpose, which easing, and how fast.
rules.why: The Animation Decision Framework says to answer these questions in order before writing any animation code.

rules.rule: Do not animate anything people trigger 100+ times a day, such as keyboard shortcuts or a command palette toggle.
rules.why: The frequency table says 'No animation. Ever.' for this band; animation makes very frequent actions feel slow.

rules.rule: Remove or drastically reduce animation on things people see tens of times a day, such as hover effects and list navigation.
rules.why: Frequency table: tens of times/day means remove or drastically reduce.

rules.rule: Give occasional elements (modals, drawers, toasts) a standard animation, and keep delight for rare or first-time moments (onboarding, feedback forms, celebrations).
rules.why: Frequency table: occasional gets standard animation; rare/first-time can add delight.

rules.rule: Never animate keyboard-initiated actions.
rules.why: They are repeated hundreds of times daily, and animation makes them feel slow, delayed and disconnected from the user's actions.

rules.rule: Give every animation a clear answer to 'why does this animate?': spatial consistency, state indication, explanation, feedback, or preventing a jarring change.
rules.why: Every animation must have a clear purpose; these are the valid ones the source lists.

rules.rule: Do not animate something people see often when the only reason is that it looks cool.
rules.why: If the purpose is just 'it looks cool' and the user will see it often, don't animate.

rules.rule: Make toasts enter and exit from the same direction.
rules.why: Spatial consistency makes swipe-to-dismiss feel intuitive.

rules.rule: Give elements a transition when they appear or disappear rather than letting them pop in or out.
rules.why: Elements appearing or disappearing without transition feel broken.

rules.rule: Use ease-out for elements entering or exiting the screen.
rules.why: It starts fast and feels responsive.

rules.rule: Use ease-in-out for elements that move or morph while staying on screen.
rules.why: It gives natural acceleration and deceleration.

rules.rule: Use ease for hover and color changes.
rules.why: The easing decision tree assigns ease to hover/color changes.

rules.rule: Use linear only for constant motion such as a marquee or progress bar.
rules.why: The easing decision tree assigns linear to constant motion.
rules.evidence: Is it constant motion (marquee, progress bar)?

rules.rule: When no other easing case applies, default to ease-out.
rules.why: The decision tree's default branch is ease-out.

rules.rule: Use custom easing curves instead of the built-in CSS keywords.
rules.why: The built-in CSS easings are too weak and lack the punch that makes animations feel intentional.

rules.rule: Define a strong ease-out token for UI interactions.
rules.why: Given as the strong ease-out for UI interactions.

rules.rule: Define a strong ease-in-out token for on-screen movement.
rules.why: Given as the strong ease-in-out for on-screen movement.

rules.rule: Define an iOS-like drawer easing token for drawers.
rules.why: Given as the iOS-like drawer curve, taken from Ionic Framework.

rules.rule: Never use ease-in for UI animations.
rules.why: It starts slow, delaying movement at the moment the user watches most closely; a dropdown with ease-in at 300ms feels slower than ease-out at the same 300ms.
rules.evidence: Never use ease-in for UI animations.

rules.rule: Do not invent easing curves from scratch; pick stronger variants of standard easings from easing.dev or easings.co.
rules.why: The source points to these as easing curve resources.

rules.rule: Make button press feedback last 100-160ms.
rules.why: Duration table for button press feedback.

rules.rule: Make tooltips and small popovers animate in 125-200ms.
rules.why: Duration table for tooltips and small popovers.

rules.rule: Make dropdowns and selects animate in 150-250ms.
rules.why: Duration table for dropdowns and selects.

rules.rule: Make modals and drawers animate in 200-500ms.
rules.why: Duration table for modals and drawers.

rules.rule: Allow marketing and explanatory animations to run longer than UI animations.
rules.why: Duration table: marketing/explanatory can be longer.

rules.rule: Keep UI animations under 300ms; if a UI element's animation is longer, reduce it to 150-250ms.
rules.why: A 180ms dropdown feels more responsive than a 400ms one; the review checklist flags durations over 300ms.
rules.evidence: Rule: UI animations should stay under 300ms.

rules.rule: Make loading spinners spin fast.
rules.why: A faster-spinning spinner makes the app feel like it loads faster even when load time is identical.

rules.rule: Use springs for drag interactions with momentum, elements that should feel alive, gestures that can be interrupted mid-animation, and decorative mouse-tracking.
rules.why: Springs simulate real physics, settle from physical parameters rather than a fixed duration, and feel more natural.

rules.rule: For decorative mouse-tracking effects, interpolate the value with a spring (Motion's useSpring) instead of tying the visual directly to mouse position.
rules.why: Tying visuals directly to mouse position feels artificial and instant; a spring adds momentum.

rules.rule: Do not add decorative motion to functional displays, such as a functional graph in a banking app.
rules.why: The spring mouse effect works only because it is decorative; for a functional graph no animation would be better.
rules.evidence: If this were a functional graph in a banking app

rules.rule: Configure springs with Apple's duration-and-bounce approach by default.
rules.why: The source recommends it as easier to reason about.
rules.evidence: Apple's approach (recommended — easier to reason about)

rules.rule: Use traditional mass, stiffness and damping spring parameters only when you need more control.
rules.why: The source presents traditional physics as the option with more control.

rules.rule: Avoid bounce in most UI; when you use it, keep it subtle (0.1-0.3) and reserve it for drag-to-dismiss and playful interactions.
rules.why: The source says to keep bounce subtle and avoid it in most UI contexts.

rules.rule: Use springs for interactions people may reverse mid-motion, such as clicking an item open and quickly pressing Escape.
rules.why: Springs keep their velocity when interrupted and reverse smoothly from the current position, while CSS animations and keyframes restart from zero.

rules.rule: Give every pressable element a subtle scale-down on :active, with a transform transition.
rules.why: Instant press feedback makes the UI feel like it is truly listening to the user.

rules.rule: Never animate an element in from scale(0); start from scale(0.9) or higher combined with opacity.
rules.why: Nothing in the real world appears from nothing; scale(0) entrances look like they come out of nowhere.

rules.rule: Make popovers scale in from their trigger by setting transform-origin to the trigger position (for example Base UI's CSS variable).
rules.why: The default transform-origin: center is wrong for almost every popover; unseen details compound.

rules.rule: Keep modals at transform-origin: center.
rules.why: Modals are not anchored to a trigger; they appear centered in the viewport.

rules.rule: Add a delay before the first tooltip appears.
rules.why: It prevents accidental activation.
rules.evidence: Tooltips: skip delay on subsequent hovers

rules.rule: Once one tooltip is open, open adjacent tooltips instantly with no delay and no animation.
rules.why: It feels faster without defeating the purpose of the initial delay, and makes the whole toolbar feel faster.

rules.rule: Animate tooltips from their trigger with a short transform and opacity transition, starting and ending at a slightly reduced scale.
rules.why: The source's tooltip CSS pattern.
rules.evidence: Tooltips: skip delay on subsequent hovers

rules.rule: Use CSS transitions, not keyframes, for any UI that can be triggered rapidly (adding toasts, toggling states).
rules.why: Transitions can be interrupted and retargeted mid-animation; keyframes restart from zero.
rules.evidence: Use CSS transitions over keyframes for interruptible UI

rules.rule: If a crossfade still looks wrong after trying other easings and durations, add a subtle blur during the transition.
rules.why: Blur blends the old and new states so the eye sees one smooth transformation instead of two overlapping objects.
rules.evidence: Use blur to mask imperfect transitions

rules.rule: For a polished button state change, combine scale-on-press with a blurred, slightly faded content transition.
rules.why: The source's example of blur plus press feedback.

rules.rule: Keep blur under 20px.
rules.why: Heavy blur is expensive, especially in Safari.

rules.rule: Animate enter states with CSS @starting-style where browser support allows; otherwise fall back to a data-mounted attribute set after first render.
rules.why: @starting-style animates entry without JavaScript and replaces the useEffect mounted pattern.

rules.rule: Use percentage translate values (such as translateY(100%)) to move an element by its own size instead of hardcoded pixel values.
rules.why: Percentages are relative to the element's own size, less error-prone and adapt to content; Sonner and Vaul use this.

rules.rule: Use rotateX()/rotateY() with transform-style: preserve-3d for depth effects such as orbits and coin flips, without JavaScript.
rules.why: These create real 3D effects in CSS.

rules.rule: Set transform-origin to where the trigger lives for origin-aware interactions.
rules.why: Every element transforms from an anchor point that defaults to center.

rules.rule: Use clip-path: inset() to animate reveals; each value eats into the element from that side.
rules.why: clip-path is one of the most powerful animation tools in CSS, not just for shapes.

rules.rule: For tab color transitions, duplicate the tab list, style the copy as active, clip the copy so only the active tab shows, and animate the clip on tab change.
rules.why: It creates a seamless color transition that timing individual color transitions can never achieve.

rules.rule: Build hold-to-delete with a colored overlay clipped to inset(0 100% 0 0) that transitions to inset(0 0 0 0) over 2s linear on :active, snaps back in 200ms ease-out on release, and scales the button to 0.97 on press.
rules.why: Slow where the user is deciding, fast where the system responds, with press feedback.

rules.rule: Reveal images on scroll by animating clip-path from inset(0 0 100% 0) to inset(0 0 0 0) when they enter the viewport, triggering once.
rules.why: The source's image reveal pattern using IntersectionObserver or useInView.

rules.rule: Build before/after comparison sliders by overlaying two images and changing the right inset of the top image's clip-path with the drag position.
rules.why: No extra DOM elements are needed and it is fully hardware-accelerated.

rules.rule: Dismiss on a quick flick: compute velocity as distance divided by elapsed time and dismiss when it exceeds about 0.11, regardless of distance; do not require dragging past a threshold.
rules.why: A quick flick should be enough.

rules.rule: Apply damping when someone drags past a natural boundary, so the further they drag the less the element moves.
rules.why: Things in real life don't suddenly stop; they slow down first.

rules.rule: Once dragging starts, capture all pointer events on the dragged element.
rules.why: Dragging continues even if the pointer leaves the element bounds.

rules.rule: Ignore additional touch points after the first drag begins.
rules.why: Otherwise switching fingers mid-drag makes the element jump to the new position.

rules.rule: Allow drags beyond the limit with increasing friction instead of blocking them with a hard stop.
rules.why: It feels more natural than hitting an invisible wall.

rules.rule: Animate only transform and opacity; do not animate padding, margin, height or width.
rules.why: Transform and opacity skip layout and paint and run on the GPU; the others trigger all three rendering steps.

rules.rule: Never use transition: all; name the exact properties being transitioned.
rules.why: The review table says to specify exact properties and avoid `all`; the review checklist flags `transition: all` as an issue.

rules.rule: During drags or frequent updates, set transform directly on the moving element instead of updating a CSS variable on its container.
rules.why: CSS variables are inherited, so changing one on a parent recalculates styles for all children.

rules.rule: In Framer Motion, animate the full transform string instead of the x, y or scale shorthands when the animation must stay smooth under load.
rules.why: The shorthands use requestAnimationFrame on the main thread and are not hardware-accelerated, so they drop frames under load; the review checklist flags Framer Motion x/y props under load.

rules.rule: Use CSS animations for predetermined animations and JavaScript for dynamic, interruptible ones.
rules.why: CSS animations run off the main thread and stay smooth while the browser is busy; requestAnimationFrame animations drop frames.
rules.evidence: CSS animations beat JS under load

rules.rule: Use the Web Animations API when you need programmatic control of CSS-performance animations.
rules.why: It is hardware-accelerated, interruptible and needs no library.
rules.evidence: Use WAAPI for programmatic CSS animations

rules.rule: Under prefers-reduced-motion, keep fewer and gentler animations rather than none: keep opacity and color transitions that aid comprehension and remove movement and position animations.
rules.why: Animations can cause motion sickness, but reduced motion does not mean zero motion.

rules.rule: In React, read useReducedMotion and swap position-based values for static ones when it is on.
rules.why: The source's React pattern for reduced motion.

rules.rule: Gate hover animations behind a hover-capable, fine-pointer media query.
rules.why: Touch devices trigger hover on tap, causing false positives.

rules.rule: Make components adoptable with minimal setup: no hooks, no context, one component mounted once and a function callable from anywhere.
rules.why: The less friction to adopt, the more people will use it.

rules.rule: Invest in excellent defaults (easing, timing, visual design) before adding options; ship beautiful out of the box.
rules.why: Most users never customize.
rules.evidence: Good defaults matter more than options.

rules.rule: Give components a memorable name, trading some discoverability for memorability when appropriate.
rules.why: Naming creates identity; 'Sonner' feels more elegant than 'react-toast'.

rules.rule: Pause toast timers while the tab is hidden.
rules.why: Handling edge cases invisibly is part of what makes a component loved.

rules.rule: Fill the gaps between stacked toasts with pseudo-elements so hover state is kept while moving between them.
rules.why: Handle edge cases invisibly; users never notice, and that is right.

rules.rule: Build an interactive documentation site where people can touch and play with the component, with ready-to-use code snippets.
rules.why: Interactive examples lower the barrier to adoption.

rules.rule: Match animation easing and duration to the component's personality and the surrounding design: bouncier for playful components, crisp and fast for a professional dashboard.
rules.why: Cohesion makes animation satisfying; Sonner's motion, design, page and name are in harmony.

rules.rule: When items enter and exit a list, tune the opacity change against the height animation by trial and error until it feels right.
rules.why: There is no formula for the opacity + height combination.

rules.rule: Review animations again the next day with fresh eyes.
rules.why: You notice imperfections the next day that you missed during development.
rules.evidence: Review your work the next day

rules.rule: Make deliberate actions slow and responses fast: slow where the user is deciding (hold-to-delete 2s linear), snappy where the system responds (release 200ms ease-out).
rules.why: Pressing should be deliberate but release should always be snappy.

rules.rule: Make exits faster than entrances instead of using the same speed for both.
rules.why: The review checklist flags the same enter/exit transition speed as an issue; the source's reason is to be slow where the user is deciding and fast where the system is responding.

rules.rule: Stagger elements that enter together, with 30-80ms between items.
rules.why: A cascade feels more natural than everything appearing at once, and the review checklist flags elements all appearing at once; long delays make the interface feel slow.

rules.rule: Never block interaction while a stagger animation is playing.
rules.why: Stagger is decorative.

rules.rule: Test animations in slow motion (2-5x the normal duration, or the DevTools animation inspector) and check color overlap, easing, transform-origin and whether properties stay in sync.
rules.why: Slow motion reveals issues invisible at full speed.

rules.rule: Step through animations frame by frame in the Chrome DevTools Animations panel.
rules.why: It reveals timing issues between coordinated properties that you cannot see at full speed.

rules.rule: Test touch interactions such as drawers and swipe gestures on physical devices (USB, local dev server by IP, Safari remote devtools) rather than only the Xcode Simulator.
rules.why: Real hardware is better for gesture testing.

rules.rule: When reviewing UI code, check for every Review Checklist issue: transition: all, scale(0) entries, ease-in on UI elements, transform-origin: center on popovers (modals exempt), animation on keyboard actions, UI durations over 300ms, hover animation without the hover/pointer media query, keyframes on rapidly triggered elements, Framer Motion x/y props under load, the same enter/exit speed, and elements all appearing at once.
rules.why: The source lists these as the issues to check for when reviewing UI code, each with its fix.

decisions.question: Should this element animate at all?

options.name: No animation
options.effect: Instant response; nothing slows the action down.
options.when: Seen 100+ times a day, such as keyboard shortcuts or a command palette toggle; any keyboard-initiated action.

options.name: Remove or drastically reduce
options.effect: Motion removed or drastically reduced.
options.when: Seen tens of times a day, such as hover effects and list navigation.

options.name: Standard animation
options.effect: Normal enter and exit motion.
options.when: Occasional elements such as modals, drawers and toasts.

options.name: Add delight
options.effect: Room to add delight.
options.when: Rare or first-time moments such as onboarding, feedback forms and celebrations.

decisions.recommendation: Decide by how often people will see it; never animate keyboard-initiated actions (Raycast has no open/close animation).

decisions.question: How should easing be chosen for each animation?

options.name: ease-out (custom, e.g. cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1))
options.effect: Starts fast and feels responsive.
options.when: Elements entering or exiting; also the default.

options.name: ease-in-out (custom, e.g. cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1))
options.effect: Natural acceleration and deceleration.
options.when: Elements moving or morphing on screen.

options.name: ease
options.effect: Gentle, even change. [inferred]
options.when: Hover and color changes.

options.name: linear
options.effect: Constant speed.
options.when: Constant motion such as a marquee or progress bar.

options.name: ease-in
options.effect: Starts slow, so the UI feels sluggish.
options.when: Never for UI animations.

decisions.recommendation: Choose by the job the motion does, using strong custom curves rather than the built-in keywords; never ease-in.

decisions.question: How long should UI animations be, and should exits match entrances?

options.name: Per-element durations under 300ms
options.effect: Button press 100-160ms, tooltips 125-200ms, dropdowns 150-250ms; UI feels responsive.
options.when: All product UI.

options.name: Longer durations
options.effect: Modals and drawers 200-500ms; marketing can be longer.
options.when: Modals, drawers, marketing or explanatory animation.

options.name: Asymmetric timing
options.effect: Slow where the user decides, fast where the system responds; exits faster than entrances.
options.when: Deliberate actions like hold-to-delete (2s linear press, 200ms ease-out release).

decisions.recommendation: Keep UI animations under 300ms and make exits faster than entrances.

decisions.question: How should springs be configured?

options.name: Apple's duration + bounce
options.effect: Easier to reason about, e.g. { type: "spring", duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2 }.
options.when: Default.

options.name: Mass, stiffness, damping
options.effect: More control, e.g. { type: "spring", mass: 1, stiffness: 100, damping: 10 }.
options.when: When you need finer control.

decisions.recommendation: Apple's approach; keep bounce subtle (0.1-0.3) and avoid it in most UI.

decisions.question: What motion personality should a component have?

options.name: Playful
options.effect: Bouncier motion.
options.when: Playful components; drag-to-dismiss and playful interactions.

options.name: Crisp and fast
options.effect: Crisp and fast motion.
options.when: A professional dashboard.

options.name: Elegant
options.effect: Slightly slower than typical UI, using ease rather than ease-out (Sonner).
options.when: When the whole product's vibe calls for it and it stays cohesive.

decisions.recommendation: Match the motion to the mood so easing, timing, design and name are in harmony.

decisions.question: What should happen when someone turns on reduced motion?

options.name: Fewer and gentler animations
options.effect: Keeps opacity and color transitions that aid comprehension, removes movement and position animation.
options.when: Default.

options.name: Zero animation
options.effect: Removes all motion, including helpful fades.
options.when: The source says reduced motion does not mean zero.

decisions.question: Should elements that enter together appear one by one?

options.name: All at once
options.effect: Everything appears together, which feels less natural.
options.when: Flagged as an issue in the review checklist.

options.name: Short stagger (30-80ms)
options.effect: A cascade that feels natural without slowing the UI.
options.when: Multiple elements entering together.

decisions.recommendation: Stagger by 30-80ms and never block interaction while it plays.

decisions.question: Which animation technique should drive a UI animation?

options.name: CSS transitions
options.effect: Interruptible and retargetable mid-animation.
options.when: Anything triggered rapidly, like adding toasts or toggling states.

options.name: CSS keyframes
options.effect: Restart from zero when interrupted; run off the main thread.
options.when: Predetermined animations that will not be interrupted.

options.name: Springs (JS)
options.effect: Keep velocity when interrupted.
options.when: Gestures, drag with momentum, reversible interactions.

options.name: Web Animations API
options.effect: JS control with CSS performance, hardware-accelerated and interruptible.
options.when: Programmatic animations without a library.

decisions.recommendation: Transitions for dynamic UI, CSS for predetermined animation, JS for dynamic interruptible motion, WAAPI for programmatic control.
decisions.evidence: Use CSS transitions over keyframes for interruptible UI

decisions.question: Where should a popup scale from?

options.name: Its trigger (var(--transform-origin))
options.effect: Grows out of the button that opened it.
options.when: Popovers and tooltips.

options.name: Center
options.effect: Grows from the middle of the viewport.
options.when: Modals only, since they are not anchored to a trigger.

decisions.recommendation: Trigger for popovers, center for modals.

decisions.question: When should a swipe dismiss something?

options.name: Distance threshold only
options.effect: People must drag far enough before release dismisses.
options.when: Not recommended on its own.

options.name: Distance or velocity
options.effect: A quick flick (velocity > 0.11) dismisses regardless of distance.
options.when: Default for swipe-to-dismiss.

decisions.recommendation: Dismiss when distance passes the threshold or velocity exceeds about 0.11.

decisions.question: How should an element's enter state be animated in CSS?

options.name: @starting-style
options.effect: Animates entry without JavaScript.
options.when: When browser support allows.

options.name: data-mounted attribute set in useEffect
options.effect: Legacy pattern that works everywhere.
options.when: Fallback when @starting-style is not supported.

process.detail: Ask how often people will see it: 100+ times a day or keyboard-initiated means no animation; tens of times a day means remove or drastically reduce; occasional gets standard motion; rare can add delight.
Write down why it animates: spatial consistency, state indication, explanation, feedback or preventing a jarring change. If it is only 'looks cool' and seen often, drop it.
Entering or exiting: ease-out; moving on screen: ease-in-out; hover or color: ease; constant motion: linear; otherwise ease-out. Use strong custom curves, never ease-in.
Use the duration table (press 100-160ms, tooltips 125-200ms, dropdowns 150-250ms, modals and drawers 200-500ms) and keep UI animation under 300ms; make exits faster than entrances.
Transitions for rapidly triggered UI, springs for gestures and interruptible motion, CSS for predetermined animation, WAAPI for programmatic control; animate only transform and opacity.
Raise durations 2-5x or use the DevTools animation inspector; check color overlap, easing, transform-origin and property sync.
Use the Chrome DevTools Animations panel to catch timing issues between coordinated properties.
Connect a phone over USB, open the local dev server by IP and use Safari remote devtools; the Xcode Simulator is a weaker alternative.
Look at the animation again with fresh eyes to spot imperfections missed during development.

process.detail: Run the review checklist and output one markdown table with Before | After | Why columns, one row per issue.

caveats: This is an AI agent skill (SKILL.md), so parts of it are agent behaviour rather than design guidance: a scripted first reply and a required review output format.
Snapshot of commit 85e8e23; library-specific advice (Framer Motion shorthands not being hardware-accelerated, @starting-style browser support) may change with later versions [inferred].

Internal tension: 'UI animations should stay under 300ms' and the checklist fix of 150-250ms sit beside a 200-500ms range for modals and drawers and 400ms toast examples; Sonner is deliberately slower than typical UI.
The checklist example 'enter 2s, exit 200ms' comes from the hold-to-delete press/release pattern, not from ordinary entrance animations. [inferred]
The 0.11 velocity threshold is computed as swipe distance divided by milliseconds in the code sample; units are not stated [inferred].
Sonner's '13M+ weekly npm downloads' is a figure the source states about the library it draws its principles from, likely the author's own (self-promotion) [inferred]; not independently checked here.
The spring mouse-tracking pattern is explicitly decorative; the source says functional displays (a banking graph) are better without animation.
The 'Initial Response' section (a scripted first reply, then nothing until the user asks a question) is persona behaviour for this agent skill and is deliberately not recorded as a design rule.
